description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de ciberseguridad y tecnología que busca desarrollar una plataforma interactiva para explorar datos astronómicos de NASA SPHEREx, comparar observaciones e identificar cambios en objetos celestes.
summary: SPHEREx observes the entire sky and publishes images every week: there are too many to review manually. A moving object (an asteroid, a comet, a nearby star) looks like just another star in a single image, but when comparing the same area across multiple dates, it "jumps" while fixed stars stay still. This tool does the work of downloading, aligning, and animating the images so anyone can spot it, without installing astronomical software.
details:
LynxScope – Project Details

LynxScope is a web-based astronomical analysis tool developed to help users explore SPHEREx telescope observations and identify potential moving objects in the sky. The project addresses the challenge of analyzing the enormous amount of astronomical imagery produced by SPHEREx, where objects such as asteroids, comets, and nearby stars may be difficult to distinguish from background stars in individual images.

The application allows users to select a region of the sky using Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates, choose a SPHEREx detector band, and retrieve astronomical observations from NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). LynxScope processes and aligns FITS images from different observation dates, then generates chronological animations and difference images that make changes between observations easier to identify. It also provides frame-by-frame inspection, candidate position lists, CSV exports, and an overlay of known stars from the Gaia DR3 catalog.

The main benefit of LynxScope is making astronomical image comparison more accessible. Instead of manually examining multiple images or installing specialized astronomical software, users can explore observations through an interactive web interface. Its intended impact is to support the exploration of potentially moving celestial objects and encourage broader access to publicly available astronomical data. The candidates identified by the application are intended for further inspection and scientific validation, rather than being treated as confirmed discoveries.

The project was developed primarily using Python and Streamlit. Its architecture includes modules for data retrieval, FITS image processing, image alignment, candidate detection, catalog integration, and animation generation. It uses SPHEREx observations accessed through IRSA and Gaia DR3 catalog data. Additional features include local image caching and a synthetic-data demonstration mode, allowing the application to remain useful when external data services are unavailable.

LynxScope is creative because it combines chronological image animation with difference imaging to make moving sources easier to notice. Rather than simply displaying astronomical images, it transforms observations from different dates into an interactive visual analysis experience. Its design was also inspired by the blink-comparison approach used in astronomical image analysis tools such as WiseView, adapted to the SPHEREx mission.

During development, we considered scientific accuracy, image alignment, changing observation wavelengths, bad pixels, external service availability, and accessibility. We also considered the importance of distinguishing potential candidates from confirmed astronomical objects. To improve reliability, we implemented image caching, offline demonstration capabilities, and tests using simulated data. The application has also been tested with real SPHEREx observations of the M101 region.

LynxScope is publicly accessible through its official website, allowing anyone to explore the project directly without installing the software.

Live application: https://lynxscope.space

Source code: https://github.com/LynxDev-Javier/planetX-SphereX
